title: Two blocs dominate
text: The story begins close to the triangle’s base: most first choices go to Labor or the Liberal–National parties. Cain’s Labor wins all three elections, with no minor-party or independent Assembly winners. The especially flat 1985 plot also reflects the choices on the ballot—the Democrats did not field Assembly candidates. An apparent retreat from smaller parties is not necessarily a change of voter allegiance.

sources.label: Australian Election Archive: Democrats’ absence in 1985

title: Independents break through
text: The 1992 shift is mainly toward the Coalition, which wins 61 seats and returns in 1996. But the dots above the main cluster hint at a second story: strong local support for alternatives. By 1999, three independents hold the balance of power and back Bracks’ minority Labor government. Support outside the major blocs can now change who governs, even without being widespread.

title: The field opens up
text: The cloud of seats begins to open upward as more voters look beyond the major parties. The Greens receive 9.7% of the Assembly vote in 2002 and over 11% in 2010, yet win no Assembly seats in these three elections. Labor’s 62-seat landslide gives way to a narrow Coalition victory in 2010. A broader range of first choices does not immediately produce a broader parliament.

title: Support broadens
text: By 2022, the upward spread reaches well beyond a few outlying seats. The Greens win their first two Assembly seats in 2014 and four in 2022. Independents also break through, but none wins in 2022. Labor returns with 56 seats despite a lower primary vote than in 2018. More first choices now go beyond the majors, while local contests and preference flows still determine the winners.
